newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Finnish ERM entry turns up political heat on Italy.
newsitem.headline: Finnish ERM entry turns up political heat on Italy.

text.p: Finland's smooth entry into Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism has turned up the political heat on Italy whose bid for re-entry is likely to be met by much greater scrutiny and caution.

In a special Saturday session of the European Union's monetary committee, Finland was given access to a club which now has 11 of 15 currencies linked to one another in relatively wide trading bands. The exceptions are Germany and the Netherlands which maintain a narrower range.

Nearly torn asunder in 1992 during a crisis which saw both sterling and the lira ejected, the ERM has been at the focus of a hot debate among those outside it, particularly about the need for membership ahead of monetary union in 1999.

Some have argued the upheaval in 1992, which led to a widening in the tradings bands from 2.25 percent to 15 percent, has weakened the Maastricht treaty's precondition of two years membership prior to early 1998.
But with Finland's entry, and the broad support it has won from economic powers such as Germany and France, political pressure is like to intensify on those not in the grid.
Such pressure is likely to be greatest on Italy.

Desperate to be among the first wave of members joining a common currency, Italy has done much to shed its image of an unreliable economic partner whose currency has demonstrated frequent bouts of instability.

Having put through a rigorous budget plan for 1997 -- albeit with a few gimmicks attached -- the Italian government of Prime Minister Romano Prodi has signalled its desire to rejoin the ERM as soon as possible.

Most observers believe Italy's timetable for re-entry is between now and year-end. With the lira continuing to appreciate on foreign exchange markets, there is every incentive to join the grid quickly.
Italian industrialists have voiced alarm at the lira's rapid advance which they believe undermines their competitive position in Europe.

But it is precisely the threat of competitive devaluation that has led France, most vocal in its criticism of Italy's turbulent currency past, to argue for an even further rise in the lira before returning to the ERM.

Lavishing praise on Finland's entry, French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis on Saturday said the decision "will facilitate the economic and commercial relations between our two countries and is a good sign ahead of the introduction of the Euro."
Italian monetary officials were silent after Saturday's EU meeting and there was no suggestion that the lira was discussed, a sign perhaps of the difficult negotiations ahead.
For apart from the rather technical debate over a correct central parity rate, there is the broader question of Italy's participation in the single currency at the start.
German Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer went out of his way last week to underscore the need for durable economic convergence among those joining monetary union in 1999.

Many analysts saw his comments as a warning to countries like Italy that their dash for economic convergence might be insufficient for membership. What was needed, said Tietmeyer, was a culture of stability.

Although his remarks may have also had much to say about the poor state of German public opinion over a common currency, they none the less raised the important issue of securing a credible launch to monetary union.
Economists say a single currency which includes too many countries runs the risk of being perceived as relatively weak.
Given all the other pitfalls which policy-makers must steer clear of in the run-up to 1999, experts say this is one they might want to avoid at all costs.
